chapter_theme: The way of one who does virtue (அறஞ்செய்வான் திறம்): virtue is within everyone's reach, a leaf for God, a mouthful for a cow, a handful before eating, a kind word; it must be done before Death comes, and austerity and virtue are the boat across the sea of deeds.
structure_note: What those who know themselves become (251); small acts anyone can do and feeding the needy (252, 253); urgency before death (254 to 257); austerity and virtue as boat and support (258, 259).

251.reading: Those who know themselves bow at the Lord's feet, stand upholding virtue and become the few who know the real; to such people the Supreme becomes their own kin.
251.nuance: தாமறிவார் opens every line. It is read here as 'those who know themselves', but it can also be 'they who know (this)'. தத்துவர் is taken as knowers of the tattvas, the real constituents; தமர் (one's own people) makes the Supreme a kinsman rather than a distant judge.

252.reading: Anyone can give a green leaf to God, a mouthful of grass to a cow, a handful of food to another before eating, and a kind word to others.
252.nuance: யாவர்க்குமாம், 'possible for all', is the verse's argument: each act is tiny, so no one can plead poverty. Worship, care of animals, sharing food and speech are set side by side as equal forms of virtue.

253.reading: Men fragrant with learned wisdom say that the food eaten by those who have nothing is virtue; those who do not feed them do not know the merit, as of one whose well or tank people come to and drink from.
253.nuance: அற்றுநின்றார் can be the destitute or those who have cut off attachment, the renunciants. Lines 3 and 4 are compressed; the reading that the giver's merit is like that of one who dug a public well is traditional but not stated outright.

254.reading: You who neither drive out your impurity and fill yourselves with knowledge nor do good while your days are full, what will you do when you lie awake as fever spreads, and what when your eyes no longer open, poor hearts?
254.nuance: விழித்திருந்து and விழிக்க அன்று frame the deathbed: sleepless in the last fever, then unable to open the eyes. அழுக்கு (dirt) may be inner impurity in the sense of malam, but the verse does not use the technical word. தழுக்கிய நாள் is taken as days of plenty.

255.reading: Before Death comes in force, which does not ask whether you know yourself, whether you are good, whether you are poor or young, do good austerity in its proper way.
255.nuance: The four negated verbs in lines 1 and 2 can describe Death, which takes no account of who one is, or the hearer, who goes on without knowing himself. Either way youth is no excuse for delay.

256.reading: For one who has renounced there is no kin from then on, for one who has died no joy, and to one who has forgotten him the Lord has not come; those who know the measure of knowing know virtue.
256.nuance: வழிமுதல் (from that point on) marks three things that end at a moment: kinship at renunciation, joy at death, the Lord's coming at forgetting. The last line can also be read 'virtue itself knows those who know the measure'.

257.reading: Those who in their austerity honour the deer-bearing Lord as God are set against the many beings who live taking the flesh as their god; to them Yama comes, saying 'I am god'.
257.nuance: மான் is taken as the deer Siva holds, so 'the deer-bearer' is Siva; line 1 is obscure. The plain point is ironic: those who serve the body get Death (நமன்) as the god who claims them.

258.reading: There are two ways that end weariness and are a boat across the surging sea of deeds: austerity and virtue, which the Lord of unfailing renown makes fruitful, are the highest support for oneself and one's kin.
258.nuance: கேடில் புகழோன் may be the Lord or the man of lasting fame who practises the two. The sea is of deeds (வினைக்கடல்), the stuff that keeps births going.

259.reading: The Lord, the support worth clinging to, does not tell the secret of release on earth except to those on the path of virtue; whatever you have given will be your help, and that is the way to take the path he set.
259.nuance: பற்றது வாய்நின்ற பற்று plays on பற்று (attachment, support) as Kural 350 does. அற்றம் can mean a secret, an end or release; line 3 (உற்று உங்களால் ஒன்றும் ஈந்தது வே துணை) is broken and the sense is a guess.

links.note: Both set the bar for giving so low no one can refuse it: the Naladiyar asks for even a fragment of a rice grain daily before eating, Tirumular a handful before eating, with a leaf for God and a kind word added.
Both make feeding those who have nothing the very form of virtue; the Kural calls it where the wealthy store their wealth, Tirumular says the learned call such food virtue itself.
Both press good deeds by picturing the deathbed: the Kural's hiccup that stops the tongue, Tirumular's fever and eyes that no longer open.
Both reject youth as a reason to put off virtue: the Naladiyar's storm drops unripe fruit, Tirumular's Death does not ask whether one is young.
Both picture a great sea to be crossed. In the Kural it is the sea of births, swum by reaching the Lord's feet; Tirumular makes it the sea of deeds, crossed in the boat of austerity and virtue.

source_issues: 259: line 3 (உற்று உங்களால் ஒன்றும் ஈந்தது வே துணை) is metrically and grammatically broken; வே may be a fragment.
257: line 1 (தான்தவம் செய்வதாம் செய்தவத்து அவ்வழி) is obscure.
